narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Afro fusion emerged in South Africa during the 1970s, pioneered by Sylvia Glasser.
It was developed as a contemporary dance vocabulary that challenged the racial segregation of the apartheid era.
The musical style evolved from earlier South African jazz and mbaqanga traditions, gaining institutional support and global recognition by the early 2000s.
on_screen: Map: South Africa · Africa
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The style originated as a response to the political changes of the apartheid regime.
It served as a means of artistic protest and a way to promote cultural diversity.
It is performed in contemporary dance theaters and at major music awards ceremonies.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance style is a hybrid of African movement and Western contemporary techniques.
It incorporates somatic practices like the Alexander Technique and release work, combined with traditional African dance styles such as kwassa kwassa and pantsula.
Choreography often emphasizes a fusion of ritualistic movement and modern contemporary forms.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Afro fusion music is an experimental crossover style blending traditional African music with jazz, hip hop, kwaito, reggae, soul, pop, kwela, blues, and rock.
Songs are frequently multilingual, incorporating African languages alongside English, French, or Spanish.
Listen for the Guitar, Brass, Percussion.
A blend of traditional African music with Western genres like jazz, pop, and rock, characterized by multilingual vocals and experimental arrangements.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Sylvia Glasser, Vincent Mantsoe, Gregory Maqoma, Ray Phiri, Miriam Makeba, Hugh Masekela, Tsepo Tshola, and the band Freshlyground.
While originating in South Africa, the style has seen significant development in Kenya, particularly through the support of the Alliance Française de Nairobi.
The style descends from a blend of traditional African dance, mbaqanga, jazz, and Western contemporary dance techniques like the Graham technique.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Afro fusion is influence of Mbaqanga: A foundational South African genre that heavily influenced the musical development of Afro fusion.
Afro fusion is influence of Pantsula: An indigenous South African dance style incorporated into the Afro fusion movement vocabulary.

music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Afro fusion (South Africa). Instruments: Guitar, Brass, Percussion. Vocal style: Multilingual, often blending African languages with English, French, or Spanish.. Form: Experimental crossover-like style.. Mood: Experimental, Protest, Diverse. It should sound like this: A blend of traditional African music with Western genres like jazz, pop, and rock, characterized by multilingual vocals and experimental arrangements. New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

tracks.use: chapters: dance it to the music

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
Traditional public-domain tunes may be used only when the profile names them and a public-domain source is on file; otherwise compose new material in the idiom.
Keep the proportions true: the meter, the tempo range and the instrument roles the sources describe.
Label every generated track with the tool, the date and this brief, so provenance is always clear.

wardrobe.policy: neutral dress with a respectful nod (palette and fabric only): the sources describe sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire, or the dance is sacred
care: every element traceable to the costume notes or a licensed image; nothing added for effect
no caricature, no exaggeration, no mixing of regions or eras
a culture bearer reviews the wardrobe before production; the review is recorded in the pack
credits name the tradition and the sources of the reconstruction
